bias_caveat: IMPORTANT: Facial emotion recognition (DeepFace) has documented accuracy disparities across skin tone and gender (Buolamwini & Gebru, 2018; Fan et al., 2023). Authenticity scores informed by facial data should be interpreted with this limitation in mind.
vocal_caveat: IMPORTANT: The vocal emotion channel is the second weakest of the four, after facial emotion, and is explicitly down-weighted. Benchmarked on 150 hand-rated clips from 6 speakers (vocal_bench/), the adopted model scores 48.9% three-class accuracy on held-out speakers - better than the model it replaced, which at 34.0% was significantly worse than always guessing NEUTRAL (p = 0.0070), but still not reliably better than that constant. No model tested beat it. Conflicts attributed to the vocal channel alone are damped accordingly, and per-segment claims should not rest on this channel. Read the within-video figure, not the headline: this report compares segments inside one video, and the channel's rank correlation with human judgement measured within a video is +0.159 across 147 clips and +0.056 on unseen speakers (vocal_bench/SPEAKER_NORM_RESULT.md). Most of its apparent accuracy is a between-video effect that says more about the speaker's habitual energy than about any individual moment.
vocal_licence_note: The adopted vocal model (audeering/wav2vec2-large-robust-12-ft-emotion-msp-dim) is licensed CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 and may not be used commercially. Every configuration measured in vocal_bench/ that showed usable signal was non-commercially licensed; the permissively-licensed alternatives measured at the bottom of every table. A commercial deployment would need to ship without this channel or replace it.

all_segments.text: Hey, it's Jason. It's been one year since I got my hand on the Google Pixel 10 Pro,
the latest flagship from a company that really seemed like it was on its last lifeline of
trying to make a phone that people would actually find interesting, and it's been a really surprising
journey to say the least. I can now definitively say that the Pixel 10 Pro is my favorite non-iPhone
and definitely my favorite Pixel up to this point. I've had so much fun using this phone,
and the past year has made me really hopeful for Google's future in this space.
And with the Pixel 11 lineup getting ready to launch in the very near future, I thought it'd
be a good time to do a long-term review of the Pixel 10 Pro, going into the specifics of what
I've loved about this phone, what I'm really hoping Google fixes, and what my long-term views
are of the Pixel as a whole, all in an effort to help you decide if the Pixel 10 Pro is the right
phone for you. But real quick, to celebrate over 5,000 subscribers to the JSL newsletter,
I'm actually giving away a brand new pair of Pixel Buds. If you guys want in on this,
just make sure that you're subscribed to the channel and the JSL newsletter. The link to subscribe
to the newsletter will be in the description down below. It's totally open for everyone. The winner
is going to be announced via the newsletter at the end of August. Thank you, thank you, thank you for
all of you who have been supporting me there. Okay, first, let's talk about the physical design of the
Pixel 10 Pro. It's kind of important because this is an area that historically, Google has kind of
struggled with. If y'all remember, the Pixel has had some very unique form factors throughout its
life. Google would experiment with weird build materials and designs that made their phone stand
out, but not always in a good way. It's kind of like they were trying to be different and cool,
which kind of worked, albeit to a very, very small population. And ironically, it's when Google just
did what most of the competition was doing that it finally found its footing. And that was with the launch
of Pixel 10 Pro. This is when they used high-end aluminum for the frame, a glass-on-glass design,
and the tested modern industrial form factor. And it finally looked and felt like a flagship phone
for today. And I don't think that you're going to get any better proof that even Google knows that
it hit a home run with this design as they didn't change anything for the Pixel 10 Pro,
despite their history of essentially throwing spaghetti at the wall with each and every iteration.
And one year later, I'll be the first to say that this is the one time that I'm glad that there's
no physical design differences from the year prior because this phone has held up incredibly well and
still very much meets the standard of a modern flagship in 2026. The robust aluminum frame paired
with the thickness of this phone gives the Pixel 10 Pro a good amount of weight in the hand that is
such a welcome change from the overly light plasticky feels of the pixels of the past, and the hardware
has stood the test of time. The signature pixel camera housing hasn't seen scratches or wear,
which is really nice because it really is the most eye-catching part of this design.
This moonstone color still slaps in my opinion. It really gives the phone a refined look and
the high refresh rate display with its small bezel still looks and performs great. And what really
has been the cherry on top is the addition of pixel snap on the Pixel 10 Pro. I have so many MagSafe
accessories. It's been fantastic being able to use them natively on this updated form factor.
All to say, Google has really stepped it up in terms of quality here as this phone is still a joy to have
in my hands. And I'm really hoping that they continue down this path with the new iterations
to come. Okay, the Pixel 10 Pro's physical design one year later, in my opinion, checks the box in
the good category, but we got to talk about another area of the Pixel that has kind of struggled in
the past when it comes to long-term use, and that's the Pixel's performance. This phone is using the
Tensor G5, Google's latest in-house processor, and the Tensor lineup so far has had a bit of a shaky
reputation when it comes to long-term reliability. The older versions were known to fall a bit short
in terms of performance, especially when compared to other flagships, and even to this day, the
Tensor isn't winning any medals when it comes to pure specs. That said, the Tensor G5 one year later to
me has been the most stable Tensor experience I've had. Even after multiple software updates and
regular usage, the Pixel 10 Pro still feels the same as it did when I first took it out of the box.
Now, granted, I wouldn't classify myself as a power user, even though I do think I push phones a bit
harder than the average Joe, but I'm happy to say that the performance on this phone has been rock
solid over the past year. Battery life has also been consistent with the Pixel 10 Pro. This was
initially an area of concern as efficiency on the Tensor wasn't its forte in earlier versions of the
chip, but the G5 seems to, again, be a lot more stable here, which has translated to good, consistent
battery performance. And probably the thing about the Pixel 10 Pro that, to me, really sets the phone
apart and still requires good performance is its ability to leverage AI. Now, hear me out on this
one, because trust me, there is no one that hates AI slot more than I do, but I really do feel as
though that the only phone out there right now that is going in the right direction when it comes to AI
integration is the Google Pixel. Gemini being the core AI assistant on this phone elevates the utility
of this device to a different level. It reminds me of the time when Apple introduced the App Store to
the iPhone. It changed what the phone could be. And even though I don't think it's at the same level,
what Google is trying to do with Gemini and the Pixel is the closest thing to a paradigm shift that
I really don't think anyone else is really getting close to. That's not to say that it's perfect,
but I really do think it's doing better than everybody else in the game right now. But let's go back to
more normal consumer level stuff and talk about how the Pixel 10 Pro has been with its cameras,
probably still the main reason why people decided to get this phone. One year later, I'd argue that the
still images this device is able to produce is still top three in the game right now. I wouldn't
even fight you if you say it's in the number one spot because the photos that you can get with this
phone are pretty incredible. And I've said this before, and it's so true, especially as I've been
using this phone over time, getting good pictures out of this phone is almost effortless. I just snap
randomly without too much thought most of the time, and I'm kind of blown away at how good these
photos turn out all on their own. Now, where I feel as though Google has the most opportunity for
improvement is with their video quality. It's never been that good, and it always feels as though
it's more behind than it actually is because the still image quality is so good. The videos that you
can get out of this phone are okay, but they tend to look over processed and too digital. If Google is
able to find a way to get the video quality on the Pixel to mirror the color signs of its photo quality,
it would be an absolute home run, especially in times like these where shooting video is a lot more
commonplace than before. But overall, the Pixel 10 Pro has been a really fun device to use over the
past year. I do notice that I play around with it a lot more than I do with my iPhone, and I'm glad
to say that's still the case today. Now, Google has leaked preliminary info on the new Pixel 11 lineup
that we'll be releasing in August. So far, it looks like it's building upon the strength of the Pixel 10,
and I'm super excited to see what it brings to the table. But if you're holding the 10 Pro, I'd wait before
jumping too quickly to get the 11 Pro. Make sure that you're subscribed to the channel to check out
the review once that phone is released so you can be informed about whether or not that phone is
worth it because the Pixel 10 Pro one year later is still a solid, solid device. But hey, that's just
me, and I want to know what you guys think. What do you guys think about the Pixel 10 Pro one year later?
Are you as impressed as I am, or are you disappointed? Curious to get your thoughts. Let me know what you guys
are thinking in the comments down below. And in case you guys missed my long-term review of the iPhone 17 Pro, definitely check it out here. You're not going to want to miss it.
